sentences.text: Ampelosaurus, a name meaning "vineyard lizard" derived from Greek and Latin roots, possessed a long neck and tail typical of sauropods and was covered in armor made of osteoderms.
The discovery of a partially articulated skeleton with a skull has made this animal one of the best-known dinosaurs in France, with the largest known individual reaching about 14 meters in length.
The genus Ampelosaurus was named by Jean Le Loeuff in 1995, establishing the type species Ampelosaurus atacis.
Abundant remains come from the Bellevue site near Campagne-sur-Aude, and by 2005, more than 500 bones had been attributed to the species.
Histological studies indicate that Ampelosaurus exhibited a slowed growth rate, a trait associated with island environments, where the onset of growth was clearly delayed compared to other sauropods.
The animal has not been found to possess EFS, which are external fibrolamellar systems common in non-titanosaurian sauropods.
In 2018, Díez Díaz et al. placed Ampelosaurus in the clade Lirainosaurinae, classifying it as a moderate-sized titanosaur from the early Maastrichtian period within the family Nemegtosauridae.
Ampelosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous Period, specifically the Early Maastrichtian epoch, approximately 71.5 million years ago.

Fossils were recovered from the lower levels of the Marnes Rouges Inférieures Formation, dating to approximately 70 million years ago, on the Ibero-Armorican Island that included much of modern-day France and the Iberian Peninsula.

A 2012 study suggested that Bellevue contained three morphotypes of titanosaurs, with one tentatively assigned to the genus Lirainosaurus. In 2021, researchers agreed that a second titanosaur existed at Bellevue but suggested it was more similar to the genus Garrigatitan. In 2023, preliminary results confirmed the presence of a new titanosaur species at Bellevue, with the description still in progress. In 2019, researchers reattributed a braincase previously tentatively linked to Ampelosaurus to the species Lohuecotitan pandafilandi.
